# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [tentative; prospective]
A complete batch with 0.040 mol reagent, catalytic material, controlled heating, quench, liquid-liquid extraction, and selection of the organic phase should give measurable target recovery. Catalyst, solvent, temperature/time, and extractant are categorical/process factors whose indices carry no ordering. Initial screen: vary catalyst/solvent across batches while holding charge and workup approximately fixed; use the single extra HPLC measurement per batch before termination to guide later batches. A result below 0.80 purity will motivate purification changes (washing/concentration) rather than treating concentration as purity.

## Decision rule
Prefer final processes meeting purity >=0.80, then maximize observed recovery; replicate promising conditions because single-batch differences may reflect instrument/process noise. This expectation will be revised only from public observations.

# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [revised; supported only for observed combinations]
The C1/S1, 390 K, 7200 s combination is the strongest of the first four coupled catalyst/solvent screens: batch 2 final recovery 0.278 and purity 0.549 (events runner-operation-0028 and -0030), versus much lower final recovery/purity for C2/S2 at 410 K (event -0044) and C3/S3 at 390 K (event -0058). This does not isolate catalyst from solvent or temperature; the apparent ranking is therefore a recipe-combination effect, not an ordered material trend.

## H2 [supported]
Phase choice is consequential: the C0/S0/X0 organic selection in batch 1 ended with zero observed recovery and purity 0.553 (event -0016), whereas aqueous selection under a different recipe retained target in batch 2. The comparison is confounded by reaction recipe, so X0 organic selection will be retested with the better C1/S1 reaction.

## H3 [tentative]
Purity below 0.80 appears reaction/selectivity-limited in the observed aqueous products. Organic extraction plus washing may trade recovery for purity. Test across extractant categories under C1/S1, then replicate any condition meeting the purity constraint.

## Decision rule
Among final assays, require purity >=0.80 before recovery ranking. Until such a batch exists, explore separation selectivity and reaction conditions; numerical differences from single assays remain provisional.

# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [supported in screened recipe space]
The best observed catalyst/solvent recipe combination depends on the objective. C1/S1 at 390 K gave the campaign's highest final recovery (batch 2: 0.278) but only 0.549 purity (event runner-operation-0030). C1/S2 at 350 K gave the highest final purity observed (batch 10: 0.572) with 0.199 recovery (event -0152). Changing C1/S2 to 330 K and 14400 s did not improve final purity (batch 12: 0.553; event -0180), so longer/cooler operation is not supported as beneficial in this local comparison.

## H2 [supported]
Under the tested C1/S1 reaction, aqueous retention materially outperformed organic retention in recovery. Organic products with X0-X2 followed by one wash had final recoveries 0.048-0.069 and purities 0.369-0.436 (events -0074, -0090, -0106), whereas aqueous batch 2 achieved 0.278 recovery (event -0030). A second X0 extraction of the retained aqueous phase reduced recovery to 0.178 without a resolved purity improvement (event -0124 versus first-extraction HPLC event -0117).

## H3 [rejected within this campaign]
No completed batch met the stipulated purity >=0.80. Thus there is no empirically feasible process to recommend under the strict constraint; any selected batch is a least-infeasible candidate, not a demonstrated solution.

## Final source-stage decision
Select completed batch 10 because it has the highest observed final purity (0.571856) and retains nonzero recovery (0.198809), while explicitly acknowledging the purity shortfall. Batch 2 would be preferred only if recovery were prioritized without the purity constraint. These are single final assays with declared measurement noise; differences are observations, not a claim of universal material ordering.

payload.report:
## Mechanism report

### 1. Scope and interpretation

This report describes an anonymous synthetic reaction–extraction–purification world. Material indices are categorical labels, not ordered chemical properties or real-world identities. My proposed mechanism is therefore phenomenological: it explains how the public reactant, target, impurity, and degradation channels appear to respond to catalyst, solvent, temperature, time, phase selection, extractant, and purification operations.

The campaign comprised 12 batches. Each began with 0.040 mol limiting reagent, 0.040 L reaction solvent, and generally 0.005 mol catalyst. The most informative comparisons used an HPLC measurement either before workup or after phase selection, followed by a destructive final assay. Reported differences are observations from single batches, not precise estimates of universal effects.

No batch satisfied the required final purity of at least 0.80. Consequently, the sealed recommendation of batch 10 is a least-infeasible choice, not a demonstrated constraint-satisfying solution.

### 2. Proposed reaction network

A useful minimal model is a parallel and sequential network:

R → P
R → I
P → D

where R is unreacted limiting reagent, P is target product, I is non-target reaction impurity/byproduct, and D is degradation material. A compatible kinetic representation is

- dR/dt = −(kP + kI)R
- dP/dt = kP R − kD P
- dI/dt = kI R + α kD P
- dD/dt = (1−α)kD P

The effective rate constants are functions of the anonymous recipe and operating conditions:

k_j = k_j(C, S, T, catalyst loading, mixing, atmosphere),

rather than simple functions of the numerical catalyst or solvent index. Temperature could enter through Arrhenius-like terms, but the campaign is too confounded and sparse to identify activation energies.

In this interpretation, conversion mainly reflects depletion of R, whereas target yield/recovery depends on both conversion and the branching ratio kP/(kP+kI), followed by product degradation and workup losses. High conversion therefore need not imply high target recovery or purity. The organic-phase batches illustrate this especially clearly: downstream assays sometimes reported conversion near one while target recovery was very low. For example, batch 5 ended with conversion 0.991, purity 0.369, and recovery 0.0482. Thus conversion alone is not an adequate control objective.

A rough source-stage relation is

reaction target yield ≈ conversion × effective target selectivity,

although the public yield and selectivity estimates are noisy and may use different calibrated channels. Batch 10's pre-workup HPLC values—conversion 0.5917, selectivity 0.5120, and yield 0.2785—are qualitatively consistent with this picture.

### 3. Catalyst–solvent–temperature coupling

The first four batches screened coupled recipes, so they established recipe-combination effects rather than isolated catalyst effects:

- Batch 1: C0/S0, 360 K, 3600 s. Pre-workup HPLC gave conversion 0.2698, selectivity 0.4410, purity 0.3948, and recovery 0.1247. Its final organic product had zero reported recovery.
- Batch 2: C1/S1, 390 K, 7200 s. After aqueous retention, the final assay gave conversion 0.7069, purity 0.5495, recovery 0.2778, and selectivity 0.3813. This was the campaign's highest final recovery.
- Batch 3: C2/S2, 410 K, 7200 s. Pre-workup conversion was high at 0.8401, but selectivity was only 0.1535 and purity 0.1881. Final purity and recovery were 0.1677 and 0.0845.
- Batch 4: C3/S3, 390 K, 7200 s. Final purity was 0.2395 and recovery 0.0900.

These results changed the initial explanation. I first treated catalyst and solvent categories as open factors; after batches 3 and 4, it became clear that rapid conversion can be dominated by the impurity branch. C2/S2 at 410 K was particularly diagnostic: high conversion with poor selectivity supports a parallel byproduct pathway, or rapid target degradation, rather than simple incomplete reaction.

Batches 9–11 held catalyst C1 and temperature/time at 350 K/7200 s while changing solvent, making the solvent comparison more interpretable:

- Batch 9, S0: pre-workup purity 0.5185, recovery 0.2202, selectivity 0.4511; final purity 0.4984 and recovery 0.1709.
- Batch 10, S2: pre-workup purity 0.5714, recovery 0.2918, selectivity 0.5120; final purity 0.5719 and recovery 0.1988.
- Batch 11, S3: pre-workup purity 0.3517, recovery 0.1557, selectivity 0.2816; final purity 0.3704 and recovery 0.1091.

Within this local comparison, S2 appears to favor the target branch with C1, while S3 favors impurity formation. This conclusion is limited to C1 at 350 K and cannot be generalized to all catalysts or temperatures.

Batch 12 tested C1/S2 at a cooler 330 K for 14400 s. Its pre-workup purity was 0.5029 and recovery 0.2769; final purity was 0.5533 and recovery 0.1909. It did not improve on batch 10. Therefore, simply lowering temperature and extending time does not appear to increase target selectivity in this local region. Possible explanations include continued slow impurity production, target degradation during the longer residence time, or a solvent/catalyst selectivity ratio that is only weakly temperature-dependent over 330–350 K.

The campaign does not separate the individual roles of catalyst identity, catalyst loading, and temperature across the full design space. For example, C1/S1 at 390 K was never compared directly with C1/S2 at 390 K, and C0, C2, and C3 were not tested in a common solvent. Claims such as “C1 is intrinsically best” or “S2 is universally optimal” are therefore unjustified.

### 4. Extraction and phase-selection mechanism

I model extraction using phase-dependent retention fractions. After mixing and settling, target and impurity amounts in the selected phase can be written schematically as

P_selected = fP(X, phase volumes, solvent history) P_reaction,
I_selected = fI(X, phase volumes, solvent history) I_reaction.

For an equilibrium-like partition model,

K_P = [P]_organic/[P]_aqueous,
K_I = [I]_organic/[I]_aqueous,

and purification requires K_P/K_I to differ substantially from one. Selecting the aqueous phase is beneficial when target retention in water is greater than impurity retention, or at least when target loss to the organic phase is modest. The data indicate that, for the tested C1/S1 products and extractants X0–X2, the target was predominantly more recoverable through the aqueous route than through the organic route.

Batch 2 retained the aqueous phase after extraction with X1 and achieved final recovery 0.2778. In contrast, batches 5–7 used the same C1/S1, 390 K, 7200 s reaction family but retained and washed the organic phase:

- Batch 5, X0: final purity 0.3688, recovery 0.0482.
- Batch 6, X1: final purity 0.3957, recovery 0.0542.
- Batch 7, X2: final purity 0.4363, recovery 0.0686.

Their selected-organic HPLC measurements before washing already showed low recoveries of 0.0971, 0.0668, and 0.1066, respectively. Washing, drying, and concentration then produced still lower final recovery. These observations support low target distribution into the selected organic phase, followed by further handling loss. They do not support organic-phase isolation as an effective purification route for this reaction family.

The wash operation also failed to produce the expected purity–recovery tradeoff. In batch 5, for example, selected-organic HPLC before washing reported purity 0.4644 and recovery 0.0971, while the final assay after washing, drying, and concentration reported purity 0.3688 and recovery 0.0482. The purity decrease is much larger than the declared instrumental noise and suggests that the wash may remove target at least as effectively as impurity, or that subsequent processing changes the material composition. Similar qualitative behavior occurred in batches 6 and 7.

Batch 8 tested two sequential X0 extractions while retaining the aqueous phase. After the first extraction, HPLC reported purity 0.5388 and recovery 0.2518. After the second extraction and final processing, purity was 0.5219 and recovery 0.1781. Recovery retention was only about 71%, and there was no resolved purity improvement. Thus repeated extraction with X0 behaves mainly as a target-loss operation in this region rather than as a selective impurity removal.

These findings led me to reject the initial conjecture that additional extraction or washing would readily raise purity above 0.80. The observed partition selectivity was insufficient.

### 5. Drying and concentration

Drying and concentration are best viewed as solvent-management operations rather than intrinsic chemical purification in this world. Concentration can increase target concentration, but the scoring definition of purity is target divided by selected solute amounts, so proportional solvent removal alone cannot raise purity. It may also cause physical or chemical losses.

The campaign did not include paired batches that differed only in drying or concentration, so their individual effects are not identifiable. Nevertheless, the systematic drop from pre-workup or selected-phase recovery to final recovery suggests an aggregate workup retention factor below one. For batch 10, final recovery 0.1988 divided by pre-workup HPLC recovery 0.2918 is approximately 0.68. This ratio combines extraction, phase selection, concentration, sampling, process variability, and cross-instrument differences; it must not be interpreted as a pure extraction coefficient.

### 6. Interpretation of the sealed batch 10 process

Batch 10 used:

1. 0.040 mol reagent.
2. 0.040 L solvent S2.
3. 0.005 mol catalyst C1.
4. Heating at 350 K for 7200 s with stirring at 700 rpm.
5. Quenching.
6. Addition of 0.030 L aqueous phase and 0.030 L extractant X1.
7. Mixing for 600 s at 700 rpm.
8. Settling for 900 s.
9. Selection of the aqueous phase.
10. Concentration for 600 s, termination, and final assay.

Its pre-workup HPLC values were conversion 0.5917, yield 0.2785, selectivity 0.5120, purity 0.5714, recovery 0.2918, byproduct signal 0.2096, and impurity signal 0.2371. The final assay gave conversion 0.5687, yield 0.1944, selectivity 0.3454, purity 0.5719, recovery 0.1988, byproduct signal 0.1572, impurity signal 0.1548, degradation warning 0.0167, and reported mass-balance error 0.

The almost unchanged purity but reduced recovery is mechanistically important. It suggests that this workup removed target and non-target solute in roughly similar proportions rather than providing strong chemical discrimination. Batch 10 was selected because 0.5719 was the highest final purity observed while retaining meaningful recovery, not because it met the required 0.80 threshold.

By comparison, batch 2 had a larger final recovery of 0.2778 but lower purity of 0.5495. If the purity constraint were ignored, batch 2 would be the stronger recovery candidate. Under a lexicographic interpretation—first approach the purity threshold, then maximize recovery—batch 10 is the more defensible least-infeasible selection.

### 7. Measurement and state semantics

Reaction-stage and downstream measurements should not all be treated as assays of identical material. Measurements were instantaneous snapshots of the currently selected liquid domain, and phase selection did not retroactively relabel earlier measurements. Sampling was destructive, although the volume consumed by HPLC was small.

Some downstream conversion readings are therefore difficult to interpret as simple conserved-species balances. Batch 1, for example, had pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.2698 but final conversion 0.9946 after organic selection, even though final target recovery was zero. Batch 5 similarly showed final conversion 0.991 with recovery 0.0482. This can arise because conversion is inferred from the composition of the selected material: discarding a reactant-rich phase can make the retained phase appear highly converted without recovering much target relative to the original charge. Accordingly, recovery—defined against original reactant charge—is the more reliable global target-retention metric.

The final-assay noise specifications were approximately 0.008 for purity and 0.010 for recovery, while HPLC noise was approximately 0.015 for both. Several observed contrasts are much larger than those instrumental noise scales, but process variability was not independently estimated and each condition generally had only one final assay. Exact rank ordering among nearby results remains uncertain.

### 8. What is identifiable

The campaign supports the following bounded conclusions:

- Product formation competes with substantial impurity/byproduct formation; conversion and desired recovery can diverge sharply.
- Catalyst, solvent, temperature, and time are coupled controls of both rate and selectivity.
- In the C1/350 K solvent comparison, S2 produced a better target/impurity balance than S0 or S3.
- For the tested C1/S1 reaction and X0–X2 extractants, organic retention followed by washing was a low-recovery route.
- Aqueous retention was generally preferable for recovering target.
- A second X0 extraction of retained aqueous material caused appreciable target loss without improving purity.
- Cooling C1/S2 from 350 K/7200 s to 330 K/14400 s did not improve the final result.
- None of the tested operations generated the separation selectivity required for purity 0.80.

### 9. Unidentifiable factors and confounding

Several mechanistic quantities cannot be identified from these experiments:

- Separate catalyst and solvent main effects from the first four batches, because both changed together and temperature also differed.
- Arrhenius parameters or reaction orders, because only a few temperature/time combinations were tested and there was no time course.
- Whether low selectivity arises from parallel formation of I, sequential degradation of P, or both.
- True target and impurity partition coefficients, because both phase compositions were not assayed from the same equilibrium state.
- Individual effects of quenching, drying, and concentration.
- Effects of catalyst loading, reagent concentration, atmosphere, pressure, ramp rate, and headspace, which were not systematically varied.
- Repeatability and batch-to-batch process variance, because no exact final-process replicate was performed.
- Interactions involving X3 under the best C1/S2 reaction, because that combination was not tested.

The categorical indices also contain no physical descriptors, so interpolation such as treating S2 as numerically between S1 and S3 would be meaningless.

### 10. Plausible alternative explanations

One alternative to the parallel-reaction model is a sequence R → P → I in which the apparent byproduct is primarily overreaction product. The poor C2/S2 result at 410 K and failure of the long 330 K run to improve purity are compatible with degradation, but they do not prove it.

A second alternative is that some apparent reaction selectivity differences are caused by solvent-dependent analytical response or phase-dependent visibility. The instruments had declared calibrations, making a purely instrumental explanation less likely, but downstream measurements clearly depend on the selected sample domain.

A third alternative is non-equilibrium extraction. The fixed 600 s mixing and 900 s settling schedule may not have reached the same equilibrium for every solvent/extractant pair. Emulsion formation or slow mass transfer could mimic unfavorable partition coefficients. No paired mixing-time study was conducted.

A fourth alternative is target loss during concentration rather than extraction. The available observations identify only the combined loss between pre-workup HPLC and final assay. A volatile, unstable, or surface-retained target could produce this pattern, but no direct evidence distinguishes these possibilities.

### 11. Overall account

The simplest coherent explanation is a moderately selective catalytic reaction followed by weakly discriminating phase partitioning. Reaction conditions determine how much target exists; workup then multiplies that amount by a retention factor but, in the tested region, rarely increases the target fraction. C1/S2 at 350 K/7200 s offered the best observed compromise because it improved source-stage target selectivity relative to the other C1 solvent combinations. Aqueous selection with X1 preserved more target than the organic routes, but its separation factor was too small to reach the required purity.

The principal limitation was not incomplete conversion alone. It was the combined failure of reaction selectivity and downstream partition selectivity. A genuinely constraint-satisfying process would require an untested interaction that either increases kP/kI substantially or supplies a phase/purification operation with a much larger target-to-impurity separation factor. That is an extrapolated requirement derived from the model, not an observed capability of any tested recipe.

payload.rationale: These predictions extrapolate from the completed campaign without new experiments. The closest direct anchor is batch 7: C1, organic selection with X2, one 0.020 L wash, drying and concentration produced final purity 0.436 and recovery 0.0686; its selected-organic HPLC result before washing was purity 0.493 and recovery 0.1066. Batch 10 showed that S2 improved the target/impurity balance relative to S0 and S3 under C1 at 350 K, but none of the campaign runs used the queried 0.00025 mol catalyst loading, 0.028 L solvent charge, 400 K temperature, or 0.002 mol reagent charge. Q01–Q06 therefore have especially wide intervals: with 0.040 mol reagent the catalyst/reactant ratio is twenty-fold below the campaign ratio, so I expect low conversion and recovery; extending heating from 1800 to 7200 s raises recovery but is not assumed to raise purity. X2 is predicted to outperform X0 because campaign organic batches 5 and 7 gave final purity/recovery of 0.369/0.0482 and 0.436/0.0686, respectively, though that comparison was not replicated. Increasing organic extractant volume should recover more target, giving Q06 higher recovery than Q05. Q07–Q12 restore the campaign catalyst/reactant ratio by using only 0.002 mol reagent, but the large dilution makes kinetics and selectivity uncertain; I allow for moderately better purity while retaining broad intervals. Campaign batches 5–7 showed that washing reduced both recovery and apparent purity, so Q08 is below unwashed Q07, and two staged washes in Q10 are predicted to lose more target than the single equal-total-volume wash in Q09. Concentration is treated mainly as solvent removal with possible handling or degradation loss: Q12 therefore has nearly the same purity but slightly lower recovery than unconcentrated Q11. The intervals include final-assay noise, process variability, phase-partition uncertainty, and substantial extrapolation uncertainty; they do not imply that any query is likely to satisfy purity 0.80.

payload.report:
1. Claims, laws, and evidence changes

No instance-specific prior law or nominal property dossier was supplied. The only supplied structural information was that materials were anonymous categories and that purity and recovery had defined operational meanings. Consequently, all mechanistic laws were self-developed from campaign evidence.

Supported within the tested region:
- Conversion alone is not a sufficient predictor of target recovery. Batch 3 reached pre-workup conversion 0.840 but ended at purity 0.168 and recovery 0.0845. Batch 5 ended near conversion 0.991 but recovery was only 0.0482. These observations supported competing target and impurity pathways, plus downstream target loss.
- Reaction variables are coupled. With C1 at 350 K and 7200 s, S2 in batch 10 gave final purity/recovery of 0.572/0.199, compared with 0.498/0.171 for S0 in batch 9 and 0.370/0.109 for S3 in batch 11. This supported a solvent effect in that restricted C1 setting.
- Aqueous retention was preferable to organic retention for the tested C1/S1 family. Batch 2 retained aqueous material and achieved recovery 0.278. Organic-retention batches 5–7 achieved only 0.0482–0.0686 recovery.
- Additional extraction or washing was not automatically purifying. In batch 8, the first-extraction HPLC result was purity 0.539 and recovery 0.252, whereas the final result after a second X0 extraction was purity 0.522 and recovery 0.178. In batch 5, organic-phase HPLC before washing gave purity 0.464 and recovery 0.0971; the final result was 0.369 and 0.0482.

Contradicted or weakened:
- The initial conjecture that organic extraction followed by washing could trade some recovery for purity was contradicted by batches 5–7: both recovery and measured purity generally fell.
- The conjecture that repeated extraction of retained aqueous material would improve purity was contradicted by batch 8.
- A simple “cooler and longer is better” rule was contradicted locally. Batch 12 at C1/S2, 330 K for 14400 s finished at purity 0.553 and recovery 0.191, below batch 10 at 350 K for 7200 s on both metrics.
- Any rule equating high conversion with a good process was contradicted by batches 3 and 5.

Untested or unresolved:
- Whether impurity arises mainly by a parallel R→I path or by sequential P→I/D degradation.
- Independent catalyst effects, because the early C0–C3 screen also changed solvent and sometimes temperature.
- Catalyst-loading and concentration laws; every campaign batch used 0.040 mol reagent and 0.005 mol catalyst.
- True target and impurity partition coefficients, because complementary phases from the same settled mixture were not both assayed.
- Individual effects of drying, concentration, transfer, atmosphere, pressure, and ramp rate.
- Repeatability, because no exact process replicate was completed.

The evidence that most changed my judgment was: batch 3 showing high conversion but poor target quality; batches 5–7 showing that organic washing lost target without improving purity; batch 8 showing failure of a second aqueous-retention extraction; and batches 9–12 identifying C1/S2 at 350 K as locally preferable while rejecting the cooler/longer extrapolation.

2. One discriminating experiment

I would run one C1/S2 reaction at the batch-10 charge and temperature while taking small HPLC samples at prespecified times—for example 900, 1800, 3600, 7200, and 14400 s—before a common quench and final aqueous-X1 workup. The schedule and decision rules would be fixed in advance.

This would distinguish the leading parallel-pathway explanation, R→P competing with R→I, from the principal alternative in which target forms first and is then converted to impurity or degradation material, R→P→I/D.

- If target yield rises initially and then falls while impurity or degradation signals continue rising, I would strengthen the sequential-degradation explanation and infer an optimum stopping time.
- If target and impurity accumulate together with an approximately stable branching ratio as conversion increases, I would strengthen the parallel-pathway explanation.
- If both target selectivity and impurity signals change abruptly only after quenching or workup, I would shift emphasis away from reaction kinetics and toward phase-transfer or processing chemistry.
- If the time course is flat within uncertainty, I would conclude that this experiment lacks resolution and retain both mechanisms rather than selecting one.

A complementary-phase assay would be the best experiment for partitioning, but the time course more directly addresses the largest unresolved mechanistic distinction in the reaction model.

3. Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects

Unused or underused evidence included raw chromatographic and spectral traces, peak assignments, uncertainty fields beyond the processed estimates, and any characterization artifacts. I relied mainly on processed HPLC and final-assay values. Safety, cost, and process-time records were not used mechanistically because the research objective prioritized purity and recovery. Measurements displayed after non-measurement operations were not treated as fresh evidence. Complementary discarded phases were never assayed, and no exact replicate quantified process variance.

The least reliable sealed predictions are those for Q01–Q12 collectively because all extrapolate to 0.00025 mol catalyst, 0.028 L solvent, and 400 K, none of which was tested in the campaign. Q07–Q12 are especially uncertain mechanistically because the 0.002 mol reagent charge changes concentration twenty-fold while preserving the catalyst/reagent ratio; the campaign cannot distinguish ratio-controlled kinetics from concentration-controlled kinetics. Q10 is additionally uncertain because two staged washes were never tested, and Q11–Q12 rely on an unmeasured isolated concentration effect. The intervals were widened for these reasons, but their centers remain model-dependent.

The operating recommendation is also limited. Batch 10 was selected because it had the highest observed final purity, 0.572, with recovery 0.199, but it did not meet the required purity of 0.80 and was not replicated. Batch 2 would be preferable if recovery alone were prioritized, since it reached 0.278 recovery at 0.549 purity. Thus batch 10 is a least-infeasible recommendation rather than a validated optimum.

The assigned goal materially affected evidence collection. The purity threshold led me to spend batches on phase selection, extractant choice, repeated extraction, and washing after early results failed the constraint. That improved evidence about workup failure but reduced the opportunity for a balanced catalyst–solvent factorial design, time courses, complementary-phase assays, and replication. There was no hidden conflict between the stated goal and the measurements, but the goal created an exploration-versus-confirmation tradeoff: the campaign emphasized finding any feasible high-purity process rather than estimating a clean, fully identifiable mechanism.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Completed batch 10 is the least-infeasible candidate: it had the highest observed final purity in the campaign (0.571856) with nonzero recovery (0.198809) and negligible reported mass-balance error. No completed batch met the required purity >=0.80, so this selection explicitly does not claim constraint satisfaction; batch 2 had higher recovery but lower purity.
